Project Earworm / Experiment 08 / Competing accounts

The memory often ranks first.
The reader still rejects it.

Removing the fixed coverage rule exposed a support-calibration problem. The new reader accepted the correct memory in 164/576 held-out cases, compared with 198/576 for the frozen Experiment07 reader. This is not a retrieval improvement.

September 19, 2026 · 16 held-out phrase groups · 4–10 events · 16 seconds of intervening sound · Existing local Mac setup · Paid external compute: $0

Absent-source false acceptances
Observed rate; 16 clustered groups

The useful boundary: the frozen system can often propose the right correspondence under an edit, but its support rule rejects most damaged phrases. It can preserve uncertainty about a weak observation in a small accepted subset. It has not achieved the requested combination of accepted memory retrieval and causal restraint under masking.

What changed

Each memory keeps the unchanged Experiment05 acoustic description: event pitches and onsets alongside time-preserving energy and spectral traces. The new matcher proposes several monotonic alignments, allowing deletions, insertions, pitch changes, and timing changes. It receives no edit label, expected note count, fixed coverage fraction, or generator pitch sequence.

A small regularized linear readout fits 12 audio-derived alignment features using four development groups. A separate four-group calibration set selects one support threshold under a 5% empirical absent-source false-acceptance ceiling. Everything is frozen before extraction of the 16 evaluation groups. The three stacked edit families never enter fitting or calibration.

The edit vocabulary, quality filters, alignment costs, and acoustic evidence rules are supplied by us. Only the small readout is fitted. MERT stays unchanged and is not invoked in this experiment. This does not establish learned perceptual identity or subjective listening.

The three control families

ControlWhat was testedWhat it established
Counts, gaps, and mixed edits4, 6, 8, and 10 events; missing notes with retained or closed gaps; multiple omissions; insertions; unchanged-count deletion-plus-insertion; wrong sources with matching length and timing; legitimate pauses.Event count alone rejects everything at its calibrated threshold. Envelope matching has 40/576 absent-source false accepts. Neither reproduces reliable retrieval.
Observation failureWeak notes, masking with a note present or absent, and events that merge in the unchanged detector.Eight accepted weak-note cases keep a missing correspondence unresolved because energy remains. All 64 masked cases are rejected. Masking robustness is unproven.
Genuine ambiguityTwo different reference phrases generate exactly the same query waveform when their differing event is omitted. Evaluate both memory orders.The new reader returns the exact pair for 4/16 unique cases (8/32 order trials), rejecting the other 12. The old reader returns it for 12/16. No hidden unique-origin guess is rewarded.

Stacking changes, one test at a time

After the core stage, each combination was run sequentially with the same frozen configuration. Each row contains 32 queries across the 16 held-out groups.

CombinationCorrect memory firstAccepted memory + recovered edits
Missing note + transposition32/328/32
Missing note + timing change32/328/32
Missing note + detuned note32/320/32

With the true reference supplied as an oracle, all three combinations recover the programmed correspondence and pitch/onset changes in 32/32 cases. That diagnostic isolates usable acoustic information; it does not count as successful retrieval. The actual emitted decision rejects most of these memories.

A missing detection does not erase the sound

The six-event example below produces the same missing correspondence in two situations. In one, the current energy trace is quiet at the location predicted by the alignment. In the other, a very weak note falls below the event detector’s threshold but remains visible in the retained acoustic trace.

Across all eight correctly accepted weak-note cases, the output retains unresolved observation and makes no quiet-gap assertion. The eight accepted retained-rest omissions have the omitted position correctly localized and quiet acoustic evidence. Closed-gap omissions produce unresolved location evidence in all four accepted cases.

Masking remains a failure of the integrated system. The correct memory ranks first in all 64 masked-present/masked-absent queries, but none reaches the support threshold. Zero causal claims here must not be presented as successful uncertainty-aware retrieval: the system declined to support any memory.

Listen to the recorded examples

These are construction-labeled demonstrations, not human identity judgments. Audio levels are preserved, including the deliberately weak note. This does not modify the separate human listening pilot.

What competing accounts added

For the 32 pitch-substitution queries, the best alignment describes deletion plus insertion rather than the generator’s one-event substitution. The programmed correspondence appears in 31/32 retained alternative sets, compared with 0/32 best paths, when the true reference is supplied. Keeping several accounts therefore preserves an explanation that a single path would discard.

This is a conditional diagnostic: those memories were not accepted. Also, substitution and deletion-plus-insertion can explain the same observed waveform. The construction record tells us how we generated the audio; it cannot establish that one causal account is uniquely audible. Physical causes remain explicitly unidentified.

Full results and denominators

There are 576 primary queries: 18 families × two source phrases × 16 held-out groups. The same queries are crossed with source-present and source-absent histories, with 0/16-second delays and intact/reference-drop/full-reset memory controls. These variants are correlated controls, not new independent samples.

Each denominator is 32. “Joint” requires the actual uniquely accepted true source and exact missing positions/insertion count, all programmed surviving correspondences, pitch changes within 0.20 semitone, and onset changes within 15 ms. The known-source columns use an oracle and cannot be treated as retrieval. Weak/merged/masked observations also have separate uncertainty metrics because undetected physical events cannot meet full correspondence recovery. Ambiguous construction accounts are not uniquely audible causes.

The damaged phrases accepted beyond intact/transposition/timing/pause controls all come from the six-event groups. Removing a hard coverage gate did not produce a length-general support rule. Four fit groups and four calibration groups are a small development sample; this experiment does not identify a universal remedy.

Memory, causality, and availability

Batch results are identical at 0 and 16 seconds. Removing the reference or resetting memory removes all source retrieval. A durable store of at most 12 acoustic descriptions is supplied; this is not evidence for learned recurrent memory or resistance to memory interference.

84 fresh sequential replays recomputed 840 waveform blocks with no feature or similarity cache, including matched history swaps and reference-drop/full-reset controls. All reproduced the cached decisions. Four additional pairs with different future audio produced identical already-available descriptions and outputs. Query and stored descriptions remained unchanged through inference.

Each replay records sound arrival, description completion, and output availability after both matching and explanation, with actual wall-clock timestamps. The simulated online schedule gave a median 59 ms and maximum 84 ms after the completed two-second query. Files were processed faster than real time; this is not a live microphone latency measurement. The existing extractor can use the whole completed block, so no earlier framewise-causal output is claimed.

What this tells us

The next bottleneck is evidence calibration across different amounts and qualities of surviving sound. The present features often retain enough structure to propose the right memory and recover edits. The support rule does not reliably distinguish incomplete-but-informative evidence from insufficient support across lengths and observation failures.

It would be premature to add more perturbations or replace the encoder based on this run. A subsequent bounded test should focus on support calibration while keeping these acoustic traces, competing accounts, and held-out controls. This report closes Experiment08; no new experiment has been started.

The evidence concerns synthetic monophonic waveforms with supplied completed windows and an engineered event vocabulary. Real music, polyphony, continuous segmentation, human perceptual identity, and musical experience remain untested.

Reproducibility and preservation

All 12,351 previously tracked files are unchanged, including Experiments04–07 and the human pilot. The run generated 1,128 waveforms with 264 fresh base interval patterns disjoint from 1,032 earlier patterns. It extracted 1,080 descriptions; the 48 stacked development queries were deliberately unused.

The audit recomputed all 13,824 trial decisions, reproduced the 1,200-pair readout fit and calibration choice, checked PCM/description hashes and freeze chronology, recomputed selected waveform pairs, and verified handle/order invariance. A relocated copy regenerated all 1,128 identical waveforms, re-extracted all 328 development blocks, reproduced coefficients and thresholds exactly, and matched four fresh held-out pair results. No test-driven predictor changes were made.
